summary: Aloha Tower, a concrete tower on Honolulu's Pier 9, carried an automatic light from 1926 until the late 1960s and now stands in a waterfront marketplace.

structures.name: Aloha Tower
structures.note: Height: 184 ft (1975 nomination), 190 ft (1926 Bulletin), 198 ft (1934 Bulletin). Ten storeys (nomination) or twelve (LighthouseFriends). Time ball on a forty-foot mast.

access.note: LighthouseFriends lists grounds and tower as open. The sources do not say whether the upper floors are open today.

facts.agency: State of Hawaii, Department of Transportation, Harbors Division (1975 nomination)

events.note: Completed and turned over to the Board of Harbor Commissioners in June 1926
Commissioned 1 July 1926 (LighthouseFriends); automatic electric equipment with acetylene auxiliary (Bulletin 1926)
Navy took control after the attack on Pearl Harbor; armed sentries; light extinguished for the rest of the war
Green camouflage sandblasted off; tower repainted white
Coast Guard relinquished control of the tower on 20 December 1947

Beacon moved from the tower to a 220-foot television tower by 1967 (LighthouseFriends dates the move to the late 1960s; its Coast Guard technician account for 1967-1969 says the light had already moved when he served)
Beacon on the 220-foot TV tower replaced in 1975 by the present Honolulu Harbor Light on a metal pole at the end of Pier 2

wrecks.outcome: Five people adrift were assisted and towed back to the boathouse by the keeper of the Honolulu Harbor light (Sand Island), not by this tower's light

notes_for_editor: No keeper roster: the tower light was automatic. LighthouseFriends also lists keepers (Captain McGregor 1869 onward, William F. Williams, Edward E. Robins Jr. 1917-1925, Manuel Ferreira 1925-1926) for the earlier harbor lights (the 1869 harbor light and the Sand Island light). Those belong to a different light and are left out of this record; a station record for the Sand Island light would be needed. Robins appears in the story only as the Bulletin's keeper of Honolulu Harbor Lighthouse (1925); the story places that light on Sand Island by inference from the 1926 tower-light date (LighthouseFriends). Disagreements left open in the text: the first harbor light date (Bulletin 1934 gives 1858 for the first light near the site; LighthouseFriends mentions no 1858 light, only an 1851 act never implemented and an 1869 purchase); the Sand Island light's first service (Bulletin: from 1909, erected 1908; LighthouseFriends: first lit 15 February 1910); tower height (184, 190, 198 ft) and storeys (ten or twelve). LighthouseFriends' '$190,000' and '1,500 saved' figures are not checked against a primary source. The Honolulu Advertiser of 30 May 1926 is quoted only through LighthouseFriends. Chronicling America has no Hawaii newspaper pages for 1925 to 1927 matching 'Aloha Tower' (searched; zero hits). The beacon's move to the 220-foot TV tower is dated only 'by the late 1960s' (LighthouseFriends); the Billian account on the same page puts it at or before 1967. Upper-floor access is unconfirmed.
